ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a large equilateral triangle, divided by a triangular grid into a triangular grid with 6 small units on each side, so there are altogether 36 small equilateral triangles with area 1 cm^2. The shaded part is a triangle, and its three vertices all lie on grid points: the left vertex is on the left boundary, 1 unit upward from the base; the upper right vertex is in the middle of the right boundary; the lower right vertex is at the 4th tick mark from the left on the base. Reasoning: Take the lower-left corner of the large triangle as the origin, and use the unit vector to the right along the base and the unit vector upward along the left side as an oblique coordinate basis. Reading from the grid points in the figure, the three vertices of the shaded triangle are A=(0,1), B=(3,3), C=(4,0). Thus B-A=(3,2), C-A=(4,-1). The determinant area in oblique grid coordinates is |det((3,2),(4,-1))| = |3*(-1)-2*4| = 11. Since the area of each small equilateral triangle is 1 cm^2, in this coordinate system this determinant exactly gives the area of the triangle in units of the area of a small triangle, so the area of the shaded triangle is 11 cm^2.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram as a triangular lattice with 6 small side-length units, since the large equilateral triangle contains 36 unit-area small equilateral triangles. From the image, read the shaded triangle's vertices as lattice points: the left vertex is on the left side one unit above the base, the lower-right vertex is on the base at the fourth tick from the left, and the upper-right vertex is on the right side halfway up. Use oblique triangular-lattice coordinates with origin at the lower-left corner, basis vectors along the base and up the left side. Then the shaded vertices are A=(0,1), B=(3,3), C=(4,0). Compute the lattice determinant |det(B-A, C-A)| = |det((3,2),(4,-1))| = 11. In this coordinate system, this determinant equals the area measured in small equilateral-triangle units, so the shaded area is 11 cm^2.

method.method_draft: First describe the shaded triangle as a polygon whose three vertices lie on lattice points of the triangular grid: one on the lower left side, one on the base, and one on the right side. Instead of measuring side lengths, count lattice points relative to the shaded triangle. From the image, the only boundary lattice points are the three vertices; no side of the shaded triangle passes through another grid intersection. Also count the visible grid-intersection points strictly inside the shaded triangle: there are 5. Apply Pick's theorem adapted to a triangular lattice: if I is the number of interior lattice points and B is the number of boundary lattice points, then the area in small-triangle units is 2I + B - 2. With I=5 and B=3, the area is 2(5)+3-2=11 small triangles, hence 11 cm^2.
